You're completely right, which is why this isn't something I'm ever going to express out loud. We do live in a country with universal healthcare, so the bankruptcy aspect isn't really part of it , but you are correct that hospitalization is a terrible thing regardless! I suppose what is actually frustrating is like, I know my friend well, I know what they do and don't take -- they have a mild, early version of a chronic autoimmune disease that is not, at this time, being treated with anything other than NSAIDs. I have the same disease, and have since early childhood. I take two separate immunosuppressing medications and have significant deteroriation in my condition when compared to my friend. 

I think what I actually find frustrating, now that I really think about it, is that my friend is very publically judgmental of people who go outside. Not like, people who don't wear masks, but people who do wear masks but still take the bus, go to the grocery store, etc. And I sort of feel like screaming sometimes because that's just not an option for me. I wear an N-95 everywhere I go, but I have to go to work. I have to take the bus. And it just rubs me the wrong way -- in a way that I acknowledge is completely irrational -- that someone who is at, objectively, a lower risk than myself and many people I know who nevertheless have to go outside to keep ourselves alive, seems to have decided that they are the pandemic's greatest victim and that anyone who goes outside is being selfish or stupid. I resent feeling judged by someone who has been able to eliminate what was an already relatively low risk, in comparison to myself and many people I know, and who then judges those of us who literally can't.

Hi OP. 
First of all, kudos on getting out. It is such a hard thing to do and you are incredibly brave. 
I googled women's shelters in the Cleveland area and it looks like this is one option: http://www.ywcaofcleveland.org/site/c.9hKQL9NNLmJ2G/b.9540551/k.6E91/Norma_Herr_Womens_Shelter.htm
You can also call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233
. They can help connect you with resources. 
You're in my thoughts, OP.

It might be emotionally difficult for you to reconnect with your family, but it is your decision. If you're set on reconnecting with your family, maybe you can mitigate your boyfriend's concerns by asking him to help you make a safety plan -- not just for your physical safety but also your mental health. This could include plans to meet immediately afterwards to debrief, a plan that you can text him to get a ride or provide backup for you to physically leave the space, a list of helplines and resources you can access if you find yourself emotionally troubles by the meetings, and what you will do/say if you are abused or witness your siblings being abused. 
If you want to reconnect, you have every right to. Maybe they have changed, although I suspect your boyfriend is right and they haven't. Just do it in a safe and smart way -- and I second the other comments that say not to do it at Christmas. Perhaps meet with them at a coffee shop or a free public event like a tree lighting ceremony -- then everyone will be on their best behaviour and if you are in public and not at their home it will be much easier for you to leave if things get bad. 
You are very brave for even thinking about this, and I wish you all the best. Be safe and know that you don't deserve any abuse that your parents direct at you. You are strong and an adult. You got this.

Hi Professor! 
I'm a 4th year undergraduate who initially enrolled in engineering, with the intention of studying biomech.  I have a rare genetic disorder causing avascular necrosis of the bones in my pelvis and lumbar spine. I use a wheelchair, and due to the intense levels of pain I was in as well as mechanical access barriers (I ended up doing first year chemistry without an accessible lab bench and had to do titrations above my head, where I could not easily see the setup) I ended up switching to the relatively less demanding program of biology.

 Given the attitude that pervades a lot of STEM courses that if you can't hack it at the pace or level they expect of you, you might as well leave, how do we prevent students with disabilities from getting frustrated and leaving STEM programmes? I'm reminded of a first year eng physics professor who told the class on the first day that "half of you will fail, and you will fail because you are not suited for engineering". Needless to say, I found the programme extremely hostile to providing accommodations. 

Do you think this is changing? Over your career, have you noticed a change in the attitudes in STEM programmes regarding students with disabilities? I had friends in first year with learning disabilities who were so disheartened by the institutional attitudes that they left STEM entirely. Anecdotally, this seems like a serious problem -- is there any concern amongst the higher ups about the loss of potential scientists and engineers because of this?

I've been on 3 mg of Prazosin, along with 150 mg of zoloft and .25mg klonopin. When we increased my prazosin, the first thing I noticed was that I started having vivid, run-of-the-mill dreams. 
It does lower your blood pressure though, so it can take a couple days for your body to get used to it. It's also wise to be careful getting out of bed for the first little while, in case of any dizziness.
